Fig. 3 Asymmetric responses to comparisons in positive mood are moderated by cognitive load; responses without mood induction are not. From Experiment 4
Experiment 4 demonstrated that self-serving responding associated with positive mood is resource-dependent.

--- Page 14 ---
When people in a positive mood were not under additional cognitive load, they adjusted their interpretations of the meaning of a shared birthday and responded to comparison targets in a self-serving ways, replicating Experiments 1 and 2. However, when cognitive resources were reduced, it was more difficult to adjust the interpretation of the meaning of a shared a birthday and, consequently, participants did not respond to comparisons in self-serving ways. Instead, their responses were like those of neutral mood participants: They assimilated to both upward and downward comparison targets. Thus, when cognitive resources were lacking, the benefits of a positive mood were muted.
Second, the effect only occurred when individuals had adequate cognitive resources. That cognitive load derailed the self-serving responses suggests that the flexible processing of comparison targets in positive moods is an effortful process and may be a correction process (e.g., Gilbert et al. 1995; Stapel and Marx 2007). In Experiment 4, in the absence of adequate cognitive resources, positive mood participants' responses to the comparison targets were similar to the responses to neutral mood participants. That is, they were unable to make corrections or engage in reinterpretation of ambiguous information in order to avoid assimilation to the downward comparison target. This supports our suggestion of a two-step process in which individuals in a positive mood initially respond to social comparison information in a consistent manner, and only engage in effortful reanalysis of ambiguous information in order to correct for the negative influence of social comparison.
RETRACTED ARTICLE General discussion In four studies, positive mood led to self-serving interpretations of ambiguous similarity information. When participants were given ambiguous similarity information, they categorized targets in self-serving ways. If the comparison person was superior, they used the information to make the target distinctively similar, basked in that person's glory, and boosted their self-evaluations. If the comparison person was inferior, they used the information to make the target either irrelevant or only generally similar, leading to no response to the comparison target or contrast of their self-evaluations with the inferior target. Overall, this pattern of self-serving responding was not found when the preference information was unambiguous or when participants were under cognitive loaded. These studies establish that mood can determine how people interpret and respond to comparison information. These studies also revealed boundary conditions to selfserving responding that provide insight into the underlying processes. First, self-serving responses only occurred when individuals were given ambiguous or flexible information about the relation between themselves and a comparison target. In Experiment 1, when individuals were not told that they shared a birthday with the comparison targets, they were unable to respond in a self-serving manner. Likewise, in Experiment 3, when similarity information was unambiguous, they did not respond in a self-serving manner. Thus, while positive mood might provide cognitive flexibility, positive mood does not blind individuals from seeing negative information. In the absence of ambiguous information, self-serving responses did not arise. In addition, this finding contradicts an alternative explanation that our effects are the result of positive moods inducing heuristic processing and negative moods inducing systematic processing. If heuristic processing were responsible for how participants responded to the comparisons, we would expect the same level of processing of both upward and downward comparisons, with symmetric contrast (or assimilation) to both types of targets. However, positive moods led to the use of a trivial similarity cue to indicate similarity in the upward comparison condition but not in the downward comparison conditions. In addition, if heuristic processing were responsible for the effects in the positive mood conditions, then inducing cognitive load should not have eliminated the self-serving pattern. Third, we found asymmetry only under positive mood, not under negative mood. If self-serving responses were only defensive, we might have found that negative mood, an aversive state, would have led to an interpretation of information that allowed for recovery. Alternatively, if responses resulted from mood-congruent information search and processing, we would expect that negative mood should lead to asymmetrically negative responses. Instead, negative mood was associated with processing of information with greater neutrality, objectivity, and focus on the data at hand, regardless of the consequence for selfevaluations (for reviews see Bless 2001; Martin and Clore 2001). Finally, the results of the present studies suggest that asymmetric responses are not a result of using mood as a resource (Trope et al. 2001). According to this model, a positive mood can be a treated as resource to be expended in the pursuit of accurate information. If this were true, in this case, we would have expected that positive mood would have been associated with contrastive responses to comparison targets, a response that is associated with information-seeking motives (Stapel and Koomen 2001a). Indeed, in other research, the experience of self-affirmation is related to just such symmetric responses to comparisons (Johnson and Stapel, in press).
In sum, these findings support the growing body of literature showing that positive moods can create an upward spiral (Fredrickson and Joiner 2002). Numerous cognitive processes are associated with positive mood and in responding to social comparison information; among these the ability to make fine distinctions between distinctive similarity and general similarity may be particularly helpful. Individuals in a positive mood were able to convert what could be considered negative feedback (one is less attractive than another person) into positive self-evaluations. Positive mood granted individuals the ability to see a shared-birthday or a shared-artistic preference as meaningful indicators of shared distinctiveness and similarity, allowing them to assimilate to upward comparison targets. hypotheses.statement: Positive mood leads to asymmetric, self-serving responses to social comparison targets: assimilation to upward targets and contrast from downward targets.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: four experiments demonstrate that compared to negative mood or neutral mood participants, participants in a positive mood engage in effortful re-interpretations of ambiguously similar comparison targets so that they may assimilate to upward comparison targets and contrast from downward comparison targets.

hypotheses.statement: Ambiguous similarity information must be present for positive mood to produce self-serving interpretation.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: in Experiment 1, we tested the initial assumption of the model presented in Fig. 1: that ambiguous similarity information must be present in order for positive mood to lead to self-serving interpretations of that information.

hypotheses.statement: Negative mood produces symmetric contrast rather than asymmetric self-serving responding, ruling out a mood-congruency account.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: However, the responses of participants in a negative mood were expected to be symmetric: contrast with both upward and downward comparison others.

hypotheses.statement: Self-serving responding occurs only when the similarity cue is explicitly ambiguous, not when it is explicitly unambiguous.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: Because the effects of positive mood are predicted to require ambiguous information, self-serving effects were expected to occur only when similarity information was ambiguous and open to alternative interpretation.

hypotheses.statement: Self-serving reinterpretation is effortful and is disrupted by cognitive load.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: When participants were under load, the positive mood effects on responses to downward comparisons were expected to dissipate, reflecting the resource-demanding nature of self-serving asymmetric interpretations.

hypotheses.statement: Mood manipulations alone do not change self-evaluations in the absence of a comparison target.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: it was important to establish that mood, and the mood manipulations we employ, are not associated with changes in self-evaluations in the absence of comparison information.

findings.quote: A one-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) revealed that the mood manipulation significantly affected participant mood, F(2, 42) = 18.44, p < .001. Participants in the positive mood condition reported more positive mood (M = 7.20, SD = .93) that those in the control condition (M = 6.15, SD = .52), t(42) = 3.43, p = .001. Participants in the negative mood condition reported more negative mood (M = 4.98, SD = .98) than those in the control condition, t(42) = -3.80, p < .001.

consequence.explanation: The reported F is smaller than the printed group statistics can produce, so the manipulation-check claim that mood was successfully induced rests on a statistic that does not follow from its own means and SDs; the p-value threshold is unaffected because every achievable F is far more significant than the reported one.

findings.notes: The cell ns are not printed. I derived n = 15 per group from N = 45 with three conditions and error df = 42, and then re-ran the check at an unequal 12/21/12 allocation to test whether that assumption was doing the work: the reported F = 18.44 sits below the achievable interval under both allocations, so the result is not an artefact of the equal-n assumption. Innocent explanations to weigh: the F could have been copied from a different analysis, or one of the three printed SDs could be a typo (a larger SD would lower F). Note the direction -- the reported statistic is LESS significant than the data imply, which is the opposite of the direction self-serving error usually takes, and is worth stating alongside the flag.

findings.quote: the upward comparison target was rated more attractive (M = 7.33, SD = 1.19) than the downward target (M = 4.17, SD = 1.19), F(1,88) = 170.34, p < .001.

consequence.explanation: The Experiment 3 direction-of-comparison manipulation check reports a target-attractiveness mean above the maximum of the response scale the paper says it used, so the value cannot be a mean of that measure as described.

findings.notes: I RECORDED THIS ONE RUNG BELOW THE TOOL. grim_check returned `impossible` on bound_source='stated'. The 1-7 bound is printed verbatim for Experiments 1 and 2 ('rated their own attractiveness and the target's attractiveness on seven-point scales (1 = not at all attractive and 7 = extremely attractive)'), and Experiment 3 says its attractiveness measures were 'the seam measures used in Experiments 1 and 2' -- so the bound reaches Experiment 3 by the paper's own cross-reference rather than by a numeral printed in that section. That one hop is why I stepped down to highly_suspicious. The competing innocent reading, which a reader should see: the same paragraph reports an Experiment 3 mood mean of exactly 7.33 on a scale the paper never states, and the pilot used nine-point mood items, so it is possible Experiment 3 switched to a nine-point instrument and did not say so. Against that reading: every Table 2 self-evaluation cell is at most 6.75, and the downward target mean of 4.17 sits at the midpoint of a seven-point scale. Verified against the PDF (page 10) -- the digits read 7.33 in both sources. n = 48 is derived as half of N = 96, not printed.

consequence.explanation: Sixty of the 193 participants Experiment 4 claims to have recruited do not appear in any reported analysis, and the paper reports no exclusions, attrition or missing data; every Experiment 4 test is therefore run on an unexplained subset.

findings.notes: The force of this comes from the control: the identical df arithmetic reconciles to the stated N exactly in Experiments 1, 2 and 3, and fails only in Experiment 4, and by a large margin (31% of the sample). Innocent explanations that would resolve it and are not stated anywhere in the paper: undisclosed exclusions, listwise deletion on the attractiveness measure, or a typo in the reported N. The derivation assumes the two df values come from the models the paper describes (a 2x2x2 factorial and single-df contrasts against a hanging control); that is exactly what the Methods say, and it is the reading under which the other three experiments reconcile.

findings.notes: Denominator: 4 suspicious results out of 24 checks that ran, across 16 cells; the other 20 checks passed, and all 16 cell means pass GRIM. The two flagged cells share the SD 0.52 and differ only in mean. THE CELL n IS DERIVED, NOT PRINTED: N = 96 with a 2x2x2 design and error df 88 gives 12 per cell exactly, which is the strongest form this inference takes, but the paper never prints a cell n. Both Python tools capped themselves at `suspicious` because discreteness_source was 'assumed'; the self-evaluation measure is in fact a single seven-point item, which would license a higher rung, but I have left the tools' verdict standing rather than re-running with the assumption relaxed. CROSS-CHECK: R rsprite2 also rejected both cells, raising 'The standard deviation is not consistent with this mean and number of observations (fails GRIMMER test)' -- but the wrapper caps a raised exception at `indeterminate` because a raise is not proof of infeasibility (measured false-raise rate 16.2%), so R corroborates without licensing an escalation. GRIM-family results still await the editorial stage's R GRIM cross-check.

findings.notes: A 4.8% inconsistency rate is unremarkable on its own -- roughly half of clean control papers contain at least one, and these must never support a misconduct verdict by themselves. The first of the three is fully explained by a degrees-of-freedom typo (see finding pilot_selfeval_df_typo). The second, F(1, 94) = 1.50 with p = .83, has no innocent reading I could find: .83 is not the p of that F under any tail convention, and it is the p of no nearby F either; the neighbouring sentence reports F(1, 94) = .31, p = .58, whose p is correct, so .83 is not a systematic convention. The third is a small discrepancy in the conservative direction.

findings.quote: Those in the negative mood (M = 6.98, SD = .53), positive mood (M = 6.98, SD = .80), and the control condition (M = 6.82, SD = .67), did not differ F(1, 42) = .27, p = .76.

consequence.explanation: The conclusion drawn -- that mood alone does not change self-evaluations -- holds under either df reading, since both p-values are far above any alpha.

findings.notes: This is the benign member of the statcheck trio and should be reported as such. The paper describes a one-way ANOVA over three conditions, which has df1 = 2; the printed df1 = 1 is inconsistent with the design AND with the printed p, while df1 = 2 reproduces p = .76 essentially exactly. rivets_anova on the same three groups independently returned `consistent` (achievable F range [0.248, 0.321] contains the reported .27, achievable p range [0.727, 0.782] contains .76). So the statistic and the p are both right and only the df is mistyped.

findings.notes: These are individually weak and should be read as a pattern rather than as three separate charges. Ordinary explanations cover each in isolation: a df printed for a model other than the one described, a contrast computed on a pooled error term the text does not name, or simple typos. What makes the set worth recording is that in each experiment the MAJORITY of dfs reconcile exactly with the stated N and design, and only isolated tests do not -- the same signature as the larger Experiment 4 discrepancy. findings.notes: Recorded as CONSISTENT because that is what the tool returned and the SDs differ by a factor of four, which is the opposite of a copy-paste signature. The reason it is recorded at all: two hanging control conditions run on different samples (N = 141 and N = 193) produced self-evaluation means identical to two decimal places on a seven-point scale. That is unremarkable on its own -- 4.20 is near the scale midpoint where control means are expected to fall -- and no tool in this kit escalates on a mean alone. It is noted so the editorial stage can weigh it against the Experiment 4 sample-accounting discrepancy rather than discover it independently. The Experiment 2 control statistics exist only in a Table 1 footnote that the XML extraction dropped; they were recovered from the PDF.

findings.quote: Higher levels of self-evaluations relative to the control condition (M = 4.20, SD = .21) were found
findings.notes: The check ran and found nothing: 0.21 is well inside the bound for a 1-7 scale under both the SD and the SE reading, so no anomaly is established. Worth stating for context that this is the smallest dispersion value in the paper by a wide margin -- every other SD reported across all four experiments and both tables lies between .21 and 1.54, with the next smallest being .51 -- and that a single-item seven-point measure with SD .21 implies nearly every control participant selecting the same response. That is unusual but entirely possible, which is why this is recorded as consistent and not as a flag. n = 15 is the df-derived control size, not a printed value.

findings.location: Experiment 2 Manipulation check; Table 2 Similarity and Self-evaluation rows
findings.quote: The upward comparison target was rated more attractive (M = 5.98, SD = .69) than the downward target (M = 2.46, SD = .74), F(1,118) = 716.92, p < .001.
findings.notes: The paper reports no effect size for any of its 63 tests, so all three of these are our computation and are labelled as estimates. Each tool call returned `consistent` -- the value and interval are the deliverable and no benchmark was applied. Reported for the editorial stage to weigh as a SET: g between 4.6 and 5.0 on seven- and nine-point rating scales means the two groups' distributions barely overlap. The manipulation check (g = 4.89, attractive versus unattractive photographs) is a case where such a value is expected and is the right yardstick for reading the other two, which are substantive outcomes rather than manipulation checks. Before treating magnitude as a signal, note that all dispersions here are labelled SD, not SEM, and that the comparisons are between-subjects as described.

findings.quote: University students (N = 96) participated in the study for course credit.
findings.notes: The paper reports no a-priori power analysis for any of its four experiments, so verify_power_analysis had nothing to reproduce; this is the design-sensitivity question asked instead. Context, not an error: a pair of Experiment 3 cells (12 versus 12) has less than half the sample needed to detect even a conventionally large effect (d = 0.8) at 80% power. This is the ordinary situation for 2011 social psychology and is not a defect. It is recorded because it is the other side of the effect-size finding above: a design with this sensitivity that nonetheless returns g near 5 on every reported contrast is the configuration in which selection inflates estimates, and the two facts should be read together rather than separately. Two tails assumed -- the paper states directional predictions but never states a tail convention, so I did not claim one.

Recorded because a clean GRIM sweep is evidence about what was verified, and because it sharpens the two GRIMMER/SPRITE failures in the same row: the means are fine and only two SDs are not, which is a narrower anomaly than a table-wide granularity problem would be.

The SAME three groups, the SAME assumed n = 15 per cell and the SAME tool return a clean result on the self-evaluation outcome while returning highly_suspicious on the mood outcome. So the equal-n assumption and the method are not what produce the mood flag. No hand-calculation signature either: the reported F does not sit at the truncated point estimate, and 24% of Monte Carlo draws reproduce it.

Checking these at 1/n would manufacture impossibilities. Recorded as a gap in the toolkit rather than a fact about the paper.

Without a stated bound no range check can be run, and inventing one would invert the check. This matters because M = 7.33 would be out of range on a seven-point scale and fine on a nine-point one.

unchecked.reason: These are main effects from factorial ANOVAs whose error term is pooled across all cells, but only the marginal means and marginal SDs are printed. The marginal SDs contain variance from the other factors, so a recomputation from them yields a systematically different denominator than the paper's model and could not distinguish a real discrepancy from that mismatch. Effect sizes were computed instead where the group statistics allowed.

Figure extraction was not run. Both figures plot means that are also printed in Table 2 and in the Experiment 4 prose respectively, and neither caption states what any error bars represent, so nothing checkable is believed to be unique to them. Recorded so the blind spot is explicit rather than assumed away.

The XML extraction reported n_footnotes = 0 for Table 1, but the PDF shows a footnote carrying the Experiment 2 control statistics (M = 4.20, SD = .86) and a blanket 'All self-evaluations differed from the control condition at p < .05'. The footnote was recovered from the PDF and used, but this is a coverage limit of the XML path worth recording: any XML-only sweep of this paper would have missed the only place Experiment 2's control condition is quantified.

None accompany this paper in the corpus. The article's only data-availability statement is footnote 4, 'Complete data and results available from the first author', so there is no participant-level file for detect_raw_duplication and none could be swept.

The article is published under the title prefix 'RETRACTED ARTICLE' but the XML and PDF contain no retraction notice, date, or stated grounds. The reason for retraction therefore could not be read from the paper itself and is not assumed here; every finding above rests only on the article's own printed values.

hypotheses.statement: Positive mood leads to asymmetric, self-serving responses to social comparison targets: assimilation to upward targets and contrast from downward targets.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: four experiments demonstrate that compared to negative mood or neutral mood participants, participants in a positive mood engage in effortful re-interpretations of ambiguously similar comparison targets so that they may assimilate to upward comparison targets and contrast from downward comparison targets.

hypotheses.statement: Ambiguous similarity information must be present for positive mood to produce self-serving interpretation.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: in Experiment 1, we tested the initial assumption of the model presented in Fig. 1: that ambiguous similarity information must be present in order for positive mood to lead to self-serving interpretations of that information.

hypotheses.statement: Negative mood produces symmetric contrast rather than asymmetric self-serving responding, ruling out a mood-congruency account.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: However, the responses of participants in a negative mood were expected to be symmetric: contrast with both upward and downward comparison others.

hypotheses.statement: Self-serving responding occurs only when the similarity cue is explicitly ambiguous, not when it is explicitly unambiguous.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: Because the effects of positive mood are predicted to require ambiguous information, self-serving effects were expected to occur only when similarity information was ambiguous and open to alternative interpretation.

hypotheses.statement: Self-serving reinterpretation is effortful and is disrupted by cognitive load.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: When participants were under load, the positive mood effects on responses to downward comparisons were expected to dissipate, reflecting the resource-demanding nature of self-serving asymmetric interpretations.

hypotheses.statement: Mood manipulations alone do not change self-evaluations in the absence of a comparison target.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: it was important to establish that mood, and the mood manipulations we employ, are not associated with changes in self-evaluations in the absence of comparison information.

findings.quote: A one-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) revealed that the mood manipulation significantly affected participant mood, F(2, 42) = 18.44, p < .001. Participants in the positive mood condition reported more positive mood (M = 7.20, SD = .93) that those in the control condition (M = 6.15, SD = .52), t(42) = 3.43, p = .001. Participants in the negative mood condition reported more negative mood (M = 4.98, SD = .98) than those in the control condition, t(42) = -3.80, p < .001.

consequence.explanation: The manipulation-check claim that mood was successfully induced in the pilot rests on an F statistic that does not follow from the means and SDs printed beside it; the significance decision is unaffected because every achievable F is more extreme than the reported one.

findings.notes: The cell ns are not printed. I derived n = 15 per group from N = 45 with three conditions and error df = 42, then re-ran the check at an unequal 12/21/12 allocation to test whether that assumption was doing the work: the reported F = 18.44 sits below the achievable interval under both allocations, so the result is not an artefact of the equal-n assumption. Innocent explanations to weigh: the F may have been carried over from a different analysis, or one of the three printed SDs may be a typo, since a larger SD lowers F. Note the direction -- the reported statistic is LESS significant than the printed data imply, which is the opposite of the direction self-serving error usually runs, and that should be stated alongside the flag.

findings.quote: the upward comparison target was rated more attractive (M = 7.33, SD = 1.19) than the downward target (M = 4.17, SD = 1.19), F(1,88) = 170.34, p < .001.

consequence.explanation: Experiment 3's direction-of-comparison manipulation check reports a target-attractiveness mean above the maximum of the response scale the paper says it used, so that value cannot be a mean of the measure as described.

findings.notes: I RECORDED THIS ONE RUNG BELOW THE TOOL. grim_check returned `impossible` on bound_source='stated'. The 1-7 bound is printed verbatim for Experiments 1 and 2 ('rated their own attractiveness and the target's attractiveness on seven-point scales (1 = not at all attractive and 7 = extremely attractive)'), and Experiment 3 says its attractiveness measures were 'the seam measures used in Experiments 1 and 2' -- so the bound reaches Experiment 3 through the paper's own cross-reference rather than through a numeral printed in that section. That single hop is why I stepped down to highly_suspicious. The competing innocent reading a reader should see: the same paragraph reports an Experiment 3 mood mean of exactly 7.33 on a scale the paper never states, and the pilot used nine-point items, so Experiment 3 may have switched to a nine-point instrument without saying so. Against that reading, every Table 2 self-evaluation cell is at most 6.75 and the downward target mean of 4.17 sits at the midpoint of a seven-point scale. Verified against the PDF (page 10): the digits read 7.33 in both sources. n = 48 is derived as half of N = 96, not printed.

findings.notes: The paper reports no effect size anywhere, so all three of these are our computation and are labelled as estimates. Each call returned `consistent`: the value and its interval are the deliverable and no benchmark was applied. Reported for the editorial stage to weigh as a SET -- g between 4.6 and 5.0 on seven- and nine-point rating scales means the two groups' distributions barely overlap. The manipulation check (g = 4.89, attractive versus unattractive photographs) is a case where such a value is expected, and it is the right yardstick for reading the other two, which are substantive outcomes rather than manipulation checks. Before treating magnitude as a signal, note that every dispersion here is labelled SD rather than SEM and that all three comparisons are between-subjects as described.

findings.quote: University students (N = 96) participated in the study for course credit.
findings.notes: The paper reports no a-priori power analysis for any of its four experiments, so verify_power_analysis had nothing to reproduce; required_n was run instead to ask the design-sensitivity question, and that is the tool named in `computed`. This is context, not an error: a pair of Experiment 3 cells (12 versus 12) has less than half the sample needed to detect even a conventionally large effect (d = 0.8) at 80% power. That was the ordinary situation for 2011 social psychology and is not a defect. It is recorded because it is the other side of the effect-size finding above -- a design with this sensitivity that nonetheless returns g near 5 on every reported contrast is exactly the configuration in which selection inflates estimates, and the two should be read together. Two tails assumed: the paper states directional predictions but never states a tail convention, so I did not claim one.

Every one of the eight Table 2 self-evaluation means is attainable as an integer sum over 12 observations on a 1-7 scale, and every one lies within the scale bounds. Recorded because a clean GRIM sweep is evidence about what was verified, and because it sharpens the two GRIMMER/SPRITE failures in the same row: the means are all fine and only two SDs are not, which is a much narrower anomaly than a table-wide granularity problem would be.

findings.notes: This is the important control on the pilot-study finding above. The SAME three groups, the SAME assumed n of 15 per cell and the SAME tool return a clean result on the self-evaluation outcome while returning highly_suspicious on the mood outcome, so neither the equal-n assumption nor the method is what produces the mood flag. There is no hand-calculation signature either: the reported F does not sit at the truncated point estimate, and 24% of Monte Carlo draws reproduce it.

check_table refused all eight: the similarity index is the mean of three nine-point items, so its granularity is 1/(3n) rather than 1/n, and grim_test has no `items` parameter. Checking these at 1/n would manufacture impossibilities. This is a recorded gap in the toolkit, not a fact about the paper.

unchecked.location: Experiment 3, self-reported mood (M = 7.33, SD = .86 positive; M = 5.44, SD = .97 neutral)
unchecked.reason: The response scale for the Experiment 3 mood item is never stated. The pilot used nine-point mood items and Experiments 2 and 4 used a single seven-point item; Experiment 3 says neither. Without a stated bound no range check can be run, and inventing one would invert the check. This matters because M = 7.33 would be out of range on a seven-point scale and unremarkable on a nine-point one.

unchecked.location: Experiment 1 and Experiment 4 manipulation-check F statistics (F(1,43) = 38.80; F(1,110) = 259.08)
unchecked.reason: These are main effects from factorial ANOVAs whose error term is pooled across all cells, but only marginal means and marginal SDs are printed. The marginal SDs absorb variance from the other factors, so a recomputation from them uses a systematically different denominator than the paper's model and could not distinguish a real discrepancy from that mismatch. Effect sizes were computed instead where the group statistics allowed.

Figure extraction was not run. Both figures plot means that are also printed in Table 2 and in the Experiment 4 prose respectively, and neither caption states what any error bars represent, so nothing checkable is believed to be unique to them. Recorded so the blind spot is explicit rather than assumed away.

The XML extraction reported n_footnotes = 0 for Table 1, but the PDF shows a footnote carrying the Experiment 2 control statistics (M = 4.20, SD = .86) and a blanket claim that 'All self-evaluations differed from the control condition at p < .05'. The footnote was recovered from the PDF and used, but this is a coverage limit of the XML path worth recording: an XML-only sweep of this paper would have missed the only place Experiment 2's control condition is quantified.

None accompany this paper in the corpus. The article's only data-availability statement is footnote 4, 'Complete data and results available from the first author', so there is no participant-level file for detect_raw_duplication and none could be swept.

The article is published under the title prefix 'RETRACTED ARTICLE' but neither the XML nor the PDF contains a retraction notice, date, or statement of grounds. The reason for retraction therefore could not be read from the paper itself and is not assumed here; every finding above rests only on the article's own printed values.

hypotheses.statement: Positive mood leads to asymmetric, self-serving responses to social comparison targets: assimilation to upward targets and contrast from downward targets.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: four experiments demonstrate that compared to negative mood or neutral mood participants, participants in a positive mood engage in effortful re-interpretations of ambiguously similar comparison targets so that they may assimilate to upward comparison targets and contrast from downward comparison targets.

hypotheses.statement: Ambiguous similarity information must be present for positive mood to produce self-serving interpretation.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: in Experiment 1, we tested the initial assumption of the model presented in Fig. 1: that ambiguous similarity information must be present in order for positive mood to lead to self-serving interpretations of that information.

hypotheses.statement: Negative mood produces symmetric contrast rather than asymmetric self-serving responding, ruling out a mood-congruency account.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: However, the responses of participants in a negative mood were expected to be symmetric: contrast with both upward and downward comparison others.

hypotheses.statement: Self-serving responding occurs only when the similarity cue is explicitly ambiguous, not when it is explicitly unambiguous.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: Because the effects of positive mood are predicted to require ambiguous information, self-serving effects were expected to occur only when similarity information was ambiguous and open to alternative interpretation.

hypotheses.statement: Self-serving reinterpretation is effortful and is disrupted by cognitive load.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: When participants were under load, the positive mood effects on responses to downward comparisons were expected to dissipate, reflecting the resource-demanding nature of self-serving asymmetric interpretations.

hypotheses.statement: Mood manipulations alone do not change self-evaluations in the absence of a comparison target.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: it was important to establish that mood, and the mood manipulations we employ, are not associated with changes in self-evaluations in the absence of comparison information.

consequence.explanation: The manipulation-check claim that mood was successfully induced in the pilot rests on an F statistic that does not follow from the means and SDs printed beside it; the significance decision is unaffected because every achievable F is more extreme than the reported one.

findings.notes: The cell ns are not printed. I derived n = 15 per group from N = 45 with three conditions and error df = 42, then re-ran the check at an unequal 12/21/12 allocation to test whether that assumption was doing the work: the reported F = 18.44 sits below the achievable interval under both allocations, so the result is not an artefact of the equal-n assumption. Worth stating explicitly because the paper reports two tables of summary statistics from different participants, which is exactly the configuration this check exists for, and it came back clean. Within Table 2 the mean 6.81 appears twice (Similarity, Positive/Unambiguous, both directions) and 6.58 appears twice in the Self-evaluation row, but each pair carries different SDs; repeated means with distinct SDs are not duplication and the tool correctly did not flag them.

inputs.blocks: Experiment 2 hanging control with sample_id exp2_control, versus Experiment 4 hanging control with sample_id exp4_control

findings.notes: Recorded as consistent because that is what the tool returned, and because the SDs differ by a factor of four, which is the opposite of a copy-paste signature. The reason it is recorded at all: two hanging control conditions run on different samples (N = 141 and N = 193) produced self-evaluation means identical to two decimal places on a seven-point scale. That is unremarkable on its own, since 4.20 sits near the scale midpoint where control means are expected to fall, and no tool in this kit escalates on a matching mean alone. It is noted so the editorial stage can weigh it against the Experiment 4 sample-accounting discrepancy rather than discover it independently. The Experiment 2 control statistics exist only in a Table 1 footnote that the XML extraction dropped; they were recovered from the PDF.

findings.quote: Higher levels of self-evaluations relative to the control condition (M = 4.20, SD = .21) were found
findings.notes: The check ran and found nothing: 0.21 sits well inside the bound for a 1-7 scale under both the SD and the SE reading, so no anomaly is established. Worth stating for context that this is the smallest dispersion value in the paper by a wide margin -- every other SD across all four experiments and both tables lies between .21 and 1.54, with the next smallest being .51 -- and that a single-item seven-point measure with SD .21 implies nearly every control participant selecting the same response. Unusual but entirely possible, which is why this is recorded as consistent and not as a flag. The n of 15 is the df-derived control size, not a printed value.

findings.location: Experiment 2 Manipulation check; Table 2 Similarity and Self-evaluation rows
findings.quote: The upward comparison target was rated more attractive (M = 5.98, SD = .69) than the downward target (M = 2.46, SD = .74), F(1,118) = 716.92, p < .001.
findings.notes: The paper reports no effect size anywhere, so all three of these are our computation and are labelled as estimates. Each call returned `consistent`: the value and its interval are the deliverable and no benchmark was applied. Reported for the editorial stage to weigh as a SET -- g between 4.6 and 5.0 on seven- and nine-point rating scales means the two groups' distributions barely overlap. The manipulation check (g = 4.89, attractive versus unattractive photographs) is a case where such a value is expected, and it is the right yardstick for reading the other two, which are substantive outcomes rather than manipulation checks. Before treating magnitude as a signal, note that every dispersion here is labelled SD rather than SEM and that all three comparisons are between-subjects as described.

findings.quote: University students (N = 96) participated in the study for course credit.
findings.notes: The paper reports no a-priori power analysis for any of its four experiments, so verify_power_analysis had nothing to reproduce; required_n was run instead to ask the design-sensitivity question, and that is the tool named in `computed`. This is context, not an error: a pair of Experiment 3 cells (12 versus 12) has less than half the sample needed to detect even a conventionally large effect (d = 0.8) at 80% power. That was the ordinary situation for 2011 social psychology and is not a defect. It is recorded because it is the other side of the effect-size finding above -- a design with this sensitivity that nonetheless returns g near 5 on every reported contrast is exactly the configuration in which selection inflates estimates, and the two should be read together. Two tails assumed: the paper states directional predictions but never states a tail convention, so I did not claim one.

Every one of the eight Table 2 self-evaluation means is attainable as an integer sum over 12 observations on a 1-7 scale, and every one lies within the scale bounds. Recorded because a clean GRIM sweep is evidence about what was verified, and because it sharpens the two GRIMMER/SPRITE failures in the same row: the means are all fine and only two SDs are not, which is a much narrower anomaly than a table-wide granularity problem would be.

findings.quote: Those in the negative mood (M = 6.98, SD = .53), positive mood (M = 6.98, SD = .80), and the control condition (M = 6.82, SD = .67), did not differ F(1, 42) = .27, p = .76.
findings.notes: This is the important control on the pilot-study finding above. The SAME three groups, the SAME assumed n of 15 per cell and the SAME tool return a clean result on the self-evaluation outcome while returning highly_suspicious on the mood outcome, so neither the equal-n assumption nor the method is what produces the mood flag. There is no hand-calculation signature either: the reported F does not sit at the truncated point estimate, and 24% of Monte Carlo draws reproduce it.

tables_checked: Table 1 (Experiment 2) - retrieved from XML, typed, and reconciled cell-for-cell against the PDF; granularity checks could not be run for want of a derivable cell n
Table 2 (Experiment 3) - retrieved from XML, typed, and checked in full: 24 checks run across 16 cells, 8 refused, 4 suspicious, 20 consistent

unchecked.reason: GRIM, GRIMMER and SPRITE all need a cell n and none is printed. Unlike Experiment 3 the n cannot be derived: the 126 factorial participants implied by the error df of 118 do not divide evenly into eight cells (15.75 per cell), so cell sizes were unequal by an unknown amount. Running a granularity check on a guessed n is the commonest route to a false accusation, so none was run. All eight means do lie within the stated 1-7 scale bounds.
Same problem: N = 47 does not divide into four cells and no cell ns are printed, so no granularity check can be run.

unchecked.location: Experiment 4, all eight cell means and the control mean
unchecked.reason: No cell ns are printed, and the stated N = 193 does not reconcile with the degrees of freedom (see finding exp4_sample_size_vs_degrees_of_freedom), so no denominator can be trusted for a granularity check.

check_table refused all eight: the similarity index is the mean of three nine-point items, so its granularity is 1/(3n) rather than 1/n, and grim_test has no `items` parameter. Checking these at 1/n would manufacture impossibilities. This is a recorded gap in the toolkit, not a fact about the paper.

unchecked.location: Experiment 3, self-reported mood (M = 7.33, SD = .86 positive; M = 5.44, SD = .97 neutral)
unchecked.reason: The response scale for the Experiment 3 mood item is never stated. The pilot used nine-point mood items and Experiments 2 and 4 used a single seven-point item; Experiment 3 says neither. Without a stated bound no range check can be run, and inventing one would invert the check. This matters because M = 7.33 would be out of range on a seven-point scale and unremarkable on a nine-point one.

unchecked.location: Experiment 1 and Experiment 4 manipulation-check F statistics (F(1,43) = 38.80; F(1,110) = 259.08)
unchecked.reason: These are main effects from factorial ANOVAs whose error term is pooled across all cells, but only marginal means and marginal SDs are printed. The marginal SDs absorb variance from the other factors, so a recomputation from them uses a systematically different denominator than the paper's model and could not distinguish a real discrepancy from that mismatch. Effect sizes were computed instead where the group statistics allowed.

Figure extraction was not run. Both figures plot means that are also printed in Table 2 and in the Experiment 4 prose respectively, and neither caption states what any error bars represent, so nothing checkable is believed to be unique to them. Recorded so the blind spot is explicit rather than assumed away.

The XML extraction reported n_footnotes = 0 for Table 1, but the PDF shows a footnote carrying the Experiment 2 control statistics (M = 4.20, SD = .86) and a blanket claim that 'All self-evaluations differed from the control condition at p < .05'. The footnote was recovered from the PDF and used, but this is a coverage limit of the XML path worth recording: an XML-only sweep of this paper would have missed the only place Experiment 2's control condition is quantified.

None accompany this paper in the corpus. The article's only data-availability statement is footnote 4, 'Complete data and results available from the first author', so there is no participant-level file for detect_raw_duplication and none could be swept.

The article is published under the title prefix 'RETRACTED ARTICLE' but neither the XML nor the PDF contains a retraction notice, date, or statement of grounds. The reason for retraction therefore could not be read from the paper itself and is not assumed here; every finding above rests only on the article's own printed values.
